title: Stop Asking Frontline Staff to Code GL: The Case for Field-Level Permissions
summary: Frontline submitters guess GL codes and finance corrects them. The fix is not training or review - it is removing the field from their screen entirely.
body_markdown:
**TL;DR:** Most AP submission forms ask frontline staff to select a GL account, then rely on finance to correct the guess. Training and review both fail because coding is infrequent, low-stakes work for the submitter and the chart of accounts keeps changing. Field-level permissions remove the decision entirely - the GL field becomes read-only or hidden by role - while automated coding proposes the account and finance owns only genuine exceptions.


## Introduction


There is a line in almost every AP submission form that should not be there. It asks the person uploading a document to choose a general ledger account.


A warehouse supervisor or store manager is presented with a dropdown of several hundred accounts, many near-identically named, and asked to pick one. They pick something plausible. Finance changes it later. Everyone treats this as normal.


It is worth naming what happens: the system requests a decision from someone with no basis for making it, then spends qualified time repairing the result.


## Why Do Submitters Get a GL Coding Field at All?


Rarely by deliberate design. The field appears because the form was generated from the ledger’s data model rather than from what each role actually knows.


A posting requires an account code, so the field appears on the submission screen. Whether the submitter can supply it is never asked.


This reflects a broader pattern where competence boundaries are not modelled. Submitters, approvers and accountants see variations of one screen, differing in record visibility rather than authority over individual fields. Control-design guidance from[IFAC](https://www.ifac.org/) emphasises matching authority to competence, which a universal coding field violates.


## The Three Options Finance Usually Chooses Between


Faced with inaccurate submitter coding, teams pick one of three responses. All three accept the premise that the submitter should attempt the code.


Response What it assumes Why it disappoints


Train the submitters Accuracy is a knowledge gap Coding is infrequent for them, skills decay, turnover resets it, the chart changes


Add a finance review step Errors should be caught downstream Preserves the full inspection cost and can mask plausible-looking wrong codes


Simplify the dropdown The list is too long Loses the granularity finance needs for reporting and reclassification


The fourth option is rarely considered: stop asking. Remove the field from the submitter’s screen, and give the classification decision to something that can actually make it.


## Why Training Submitters Does Not Work


Training is almost always the first response, and it consistently underperforms.


Coding is infrequent work for a frontline employee. Someone submitting four documents a month has little opportunity to build or retain skill, and the gap between submissions is long enough for knowledge to decay.


It is also low-stakes from their perspective. A wrong code creates no consequence for the submitter, and the correction happens downstream and silently. Behaviour producing no felt consequence does not improve.


Finally, the target moves. Charts of accounts are restructured, cost centres added, categories renamed, and nobody retrains field staff when an account is split. Material from[the Institute of Management Accountants](https://www.imanet.org/) on process ownership makes the point: a control depending on continuous retraining of people outside finance is not durable.


## What Field-Level Permissions Actually Change


The change is narrow and architectural. Permissions usually govern which records a role can see and which actions it can take. Field-level permissions go one level deeper and govern which individual fields a role can edit.


Applied to AP, this means the chart-of-accounts field becomes read-only or hidden for submitter roles while remaining fully editable for finance roles. The submitter still completes everything they genuinely know.


Field Submitter Finance


Vendor and document image Edit Edit


What was purchased, description Edit Edit


Site, outlet or cost centre Edit Edit


Budget category Edit Edit


GL account code Read-only or hidden Edit


Tax treatment Read-only Edit


The distinction the table encodes is between description and classification. Submitters are authoritative on description: they were there, they know what arrived and where it went. They have no standing on classification, which is an accounting judgement about how a description maps to the ledger. Separating these two is the entire intervention. Our[comparison of automated and manual GL coding](https://peakflo.co/blog/automated-vs-manual-gl-coding-comparison) covers the accuracy differential once classification moves to an engine.


## Who Owns the Code If the Submitter Does Not?


Removing the field only helps if something better fills the gap. Automated coding proposes the account from the signals that genuinely predict it: the vendor, the purchase description, the cost centre, the budget category and the organisation’s own coding history for similar transactions.


A confidence threshold then splits the population into three routes, and the finance queue becomes far smaller than reviewing every submitter guess because it holds only genuinely ambiguous transactions.


Confidence band Route Who decides Finance effort


High Posts automatically No human None


Medium Proposed code shown for confirmation Finance confirms Seconds per item


Low Held in exception queue Finance classifies Full decision


The pattern matters most for invoices with no purchase order to inherit coding from, which is where submitter guesses cause the heaviest month-end rework. Our guides to[GL coding automation for non-PO invoices](https://peakflo.co/blog/gl-coding-automation-non-po-invoices) and the wider[non-PO invoice processing challenges](https://peakflo.co/blog/non-po-invoice-processing-challenges-solutions) address that population directly.


Crucially, accountability does not move. Finance already owns coding accuracy in practice, since finance corrects the errors and signs off the close. Field-level permissions align the system with that reality instead of pretending the submitter is responsible.


## How to Make the Change: A Practical Sequence


**Step 1: Audit who codes and who corrects.** Measure the share of submitter-entered codes that finance changes before posting. In organisations where operational staff code, this is frequently a majority, and the number is the business case.


**Step 2: Separate description from classification.** List every field on the submission form and assign it to one category or the other. Disagreements here are usually resolved by asking whether the submitter was physically present for the fact in question.


**Step 3: Restrict the chart-of-accounts field by role.** Make it read-only or hidden for submitter roles. Read-only is generally preferable where the submitter has some context, because seeing the proposed code lets them flag obvious mismatches.


**Step 4: Assign coding to an engine with a confidence threshold.** Set the threshold deliberately. Too high floods the finance queue, too low posts weak guesses silently.


**Step 5: Report corrections as a model signal.** Every finance correction is training data. Monitor correction rate by vendor and category to find where coding logic needs attention.

## Our Verdict: Remove the Field Before Improving the Guess


### Restrict the GL field by role when


- Operational staff outside finance submit invoices or expenses
- Finance corrects a significant share of submitted codes before posting
- Month-end includes recurring reclassification journals
- Your chart of accounts has more than a few dozen active accounts
- Non-PO invoices make up a large part of your volume


### Keep submitter coding when


- Submitters are qualified accounting staff
- The chart of accounts is genuinely short and unambiguous
- Submitters own the budget and are measured on classification accuracy


**Our Recommendation:** Treat this as a permissions change rather than a training or accuracy project. Measure your correction rate first, because it is both the business case and the baseline. Then restrict the field by role and move classification to an automated engine with an explicit confidence threshold. Teams that do this in the right order usually find the finance workload drops faster than coding accuracy alone would predict, because the inspection cost disappears along with the guess. Practical reference material is available from[Corporate Finance Institute](https://corporatefinanceinstitute.com/resources/accounting/accounts-payable/) and[ACCA](https://www.accaglobal.com/) .


## Conclusion


The instinct when submitted data is wrong is to improve the person supplying it. Sometimes that is right. Here it is not, because the submitter was asked for something they never had.


A warehouse supervisor knows what arrived, when and for which site. That knowledge is valuable and should be captured carefully. Which ledger account it maps to is a different question, belonging to people with the context to answer it and systems that can learn the mapping. Taking the field off the submitter’s screen is not a restriction on them; it removes a question that should never have been asked. Benchmarking material from the[Association for Financial Professionals](https://www.afponline.org/) helps compare coding and exception rates against peers.


## Frequently Asked Questions


**Why do frontline submitters get a GL coding field at all?** Usually because the form was built from the ledger’s data model rather than from each role’s competence. Every field the posting needs appears on the submission screen, including fields the submitter has no basis to complete.


**Is hiding the field not just withholding information?** No. It removes a decision the submitter was never equipped to make. They still describe what was purchased, for which site and under which budget, which is the information they genuinely hold.


**Why does training submitters on the chart of accounts fail?** Because coding is an infrequent, low-stakes task for them and the chart changes over time. Skills decay between submissions, staff turnover resets the training, and accuracy never reaches a level finance can rely on.


**Does a review step not already solve this?** Review catches errors but keeps the cost. Finance still inspects every line, and a plausible wrong code is more likely to pass review than an obviously blank one, so review can reduce accuracy.


**Who should own the GL code if submitters do not?** An automated coding engine should propose it from vendor, category, cost centre and history, with finance owning exceptions below a confidence threshold. Accountability stays with finance, which already carries it in practice.


**What is the difference between hiding and greying out the field?** Greying out shows the proposed code as read-only, which builds confidence and helps submitters spot obvious mismatches. Hiding removes it entirely and suits roles with no accounting context at all.


**Will this slow submissions down?** It usually speeds them up. Removing a field the submitter found confusing shortens the form and reduces abandonment, which is a common cause of invoices never being submitted at all.


**How does this affect segregation of duties?** It strengthens it. Classification moves to a controlled, logged process rather than being set by whoever happened to receive the document, and corrections carry an audit trail.


**What should we measure after making the change?** Correction rate before posting, month-end reclassification journal volume, submission completion time, and the share of invoices coded without finance touching them.


**Does this work for non-PO invoices?** It matters most there. Non-PO invoices have no purchase order to inherit coding from, so they are exactly where submitter guesses cause the heaviest month-end rework.
